title: US Ends Open-Ended Student Visas, Imposes Four-Year Cap That Hits 300,000 Indians Hardest
excerpt: The new DHS rule replaces decades-old 'duration of status' with fixed admission periods, cuts post-graduation grace from 60 to 30 days, and could cost the US economy up to $145 billion over a decade.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • DHS ends 'duration of status' for student visas, imposing a four-year cap.
  • Indian students face significant impacts, including reduced grace periods and higher fees.
  • The rule could cost the US economy up to $145 billion over the next decade.
  • International student applications to US universities have dropped by 20%.
  • The Department of Homeland Security has finalized a rule ending the 48-year-old "duration of status" framework, replacing it with a fixed four-year cap on F-1 student and J-1 exchange visitor visas.
  • Indian students — the largest F-1 population in the US — face the steepest impact, with the post-graduation grace period slashed from 60 to 30 days and new federal extension fees of $300 to $2,400.
  • The rule takes effect 60 days after Federal Register publication, expected around September 15, 2026, with existing visa holders automatically transitioning to the new four-year limit.
  • Brookings researchers estimate the change could cost the US economy up to $145 billion over a decade as international students choose Australia, Canada, and the UK instead.

A 48-Year Policy Swept Away

The Department of Homeland Security published a final rule on July 17 that eliminates "duration of status," a framework in place since 1978 that allowed international students to remain in the United States for as long as their academic programs required. In its place, F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, and I-visa journalists will be admitted for fixed periods capped at four years.

"For nearly half a century, the outdated duration of status system has compromised national security and created an environment ripe for immigration fraud," said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, framing the change as a corrective to a system he said allowed thousands to "perpetually enroll in courses to avoid having to leave the US."

https://x.com/AhmadRehanKhan/status/2078114784671670404

The regulation will take effect 60 days after its Federal Register publication. Students already in the US will automatically transition to the new system, with their authorized stay capped at four years from the effective date — expected around September 15, 2026.

What Changes for Indian Students

India is the largest source country for F-1 students in the United States, meaning Indian students are disproportionately exposed to every provision in the new framework.

Under the revised rules, students who need more than four years to complete a degree — more than half of bachelor's students do, according to federal data, and the median doctoral student spends nearly six years — must file a formal Extension of Stay application with USCIS, complete with biometric verification, background checks, and fraud screening. That application carries fees ranging from $300 to $500, with an additional $1,900 for premium processing.

"This is forcing international students to pay an extra $300 to $500 in filing fees, plus another $1,900 in premium processing if they want a response prior to five months," Danielle Goldman, co-founder and CEO of Build Talent Labs, told ANI. "The US government is saying, we believe there's money to be made here."

The post-OPT grace period has been cut from 60 to 30 days, halving the window for graduates to find employer sponsorship, transfer to another institution, or change their immigration status. David Bier, director of immigration studies at the Cato Institute, called this out directly: "International students, many of whom will have spent years in the USA, will now have just 30 days to find an employer to sponsor them or immediately be turned into illegal immigrants."

The Economic Stakes

International students contributed $42.9 billion to the US economy and supported 355,736 jobs in the 2024-25 academic year, according to NAFSA. A report commissioned by the National Academies of Sciences projected that the rule could cause annual losses of $72 billion to $145 billion over a decade — more than 22 times the $3.3 billion DHS estimated as the rule's total ten-year cost.

The Brookings Institution noted that roughly half of international Ph.D. students surveyed said they would have reconsidered studying in the US if they had known duration of status would be eliminated. The Association of Public and Land-grant Universities warned that requiring immigration officers to approve academic changes would force officials to "become experts on academic programs and systems for which they are not trained nor qualified."

Applications to US universities from international students have already dropped 20%, according to Brookings, with Australia, Canada, and the UK absorbing the shift.

What to Watch

The regulation does not specify the criteria USCIS will use to approve or deny extensions, nor does it outline expected processing times. With USCIS already managing substantial backlogs across other visa categories, immigration attorneys warn that the extension system could create bottlenecks that force compliant students into unauthorized status through no fault of their own.

Sixteen state attorneys general submitted comments opposing the rule during the public comment period, and legal challenges are expected. For the roughly 300,000 Indian students currently studying in the US, the next 60 days before the rule takes effect represent a narrow window to assess their options and plan accordingly.
